content: The Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is the causative agent of Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) and represents a significant global health burden. It is the fifth leading cause of disability across all age groups. HIV belongs to the Retroviridae family and primarily targets immune system cells, including CD4+ T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages. There are two serotypes of HIV, with HIV-1 being the more virulent and pathogenic of the two. With the advent of antiretroviral therapy (ART), HIV is now considered a chronic illness, most commonly observed in men who have sex with men. Early symptoms of HIV infection are nonspecific, but as the disease progresses to its final stage, AIDS, patients experience opportunistic infections due to severe immune suppression. HIV is diagnosed using several methods, including polymerase chain reaction (PCR), enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), western blot, and rapid antigen testing. ART has significantly improved treatment outcomes, and vaccines have shown promise in prevention. Prevention remains a cornerstone of HIV management, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends routine screening for men who have sex with men, pregnant women, individuals who use intravenous drugs, and sexually active heterosexuals. Despite advancements in treatment, HIV remains a serious condition requiring ongoing efforts in surveillance and education by healthcare providers. Classification of HIV Infection The World Health Organization (WHO) and the CDC classify HIV-infected individuals based on their CD4+ T cell count: Stage A: Asymptomatic, with a CD4+ T cell count greater than 500 cells/μL. Stage B: Mild symptoms or symptoms associated with AIDS-related complex, with a CD4+ T cell count between 400 and 200 cells/μL. Stage C: AIDS-defining illnesses, with a CD4+ T cell count below 200 cells/μL. Disease Progression In the early weeks of infection, symptoms may be nonspecific or absent. Over months and years, as the CD4+ T cell count declines below 200 cells/μL, patients become susceptible to opportunistic infections and certain malignancies. Diagnostic Approach In regions with a high prevalence of HIV, patients with a high clinical suspicion of infection should undergo a structured diagnostic approach. Common diagnostic tools include: Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) Enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) Chemiluminescence immunoassays (CLIAs) Electrochemiluminescence immunoassays (ELAs) Treatment The most effective treatment for HIV is Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART). This regimen typically includes a combination of two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) and one drug from a different class, such as: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) Protease inhibitors Integrase strand transfer inhibitors CCR5 antagonists (e.g., C-C motif chemokine receptor 5 inhibitors) Examples of commonly used drugs include tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) and tenofovir alafenamide (TAF). Recommendations for Clinical Practice Do's: Perform HLA-B5701 testing before initiating treatment with abacavir to avoid hypersensitivity reactions. Monitor complete blood count (CBC) with differentials when prescribing zidovudine. Don'ts: Avoid prescribing tenofovir in patients with renal impairment or bone disease due to its potential nephrotoxic and osteotoxic effects. Do not use nevirapine in patients with hepatic impairment, as it can exacerbate liver dysfunction.
